title: Yud
hook: the smallest letter, which begins God's name

segments.voice: Yesterday closed the week with tov, good, said over the first light. Your line was tet for good. What did you call good before it was finished? A new week starts with a very small letter. Day one thousand three hundred thirty-eight.

On a page of Hebrew, the letters sit on the line and fill the space between top and bottom. One doesn't. It hangs from the top line like a drop of water that hasn't fallen yet. A short stroke, a little hook, hardly more than a comma. You could miss it. A scribe writing a Torah scroll can't. And this tiny mark has a strange double life. It's the letter that begins a word scribes treat with special care, the name of God. And it's also the hero of a small, tender story the rabbis tell, about a letter that went missing and wouldn't stop asking to be used.
screen: `A DROP HANGING FROM THE LINE.` → `EASY TO MISS.` → `IT BEGINS GOD'S NAME.`

segments.voice: Yud. Three things about the letter tradition calls the smallest. First, the name. The holy name of God in the Torah, the one the King James renders as LORD in capital letters, begins with a yud. Jewish tradition treats that name with such care that it isn't spoken aloud as written. In prayer and in reading the Torah, Jews traditionally say Adonai, my Lord, in its place, and in ordinary talk some say Hashem, the Name. So the smallest letter stands at the front of the word held with such care. Second, a story. Remember heh, a few days ago, when Sarai became Sarah? The yud at the end of her name came off to make room. The rabbis, in the Jerusalem Talmud, imagine what happened to it. The little yud, they say, came before God and complained: I was in the name of a righteous woman, and now I've been taken out. And it kept asking, for a long time, until God placed it at the front of another name. In the book of Numbers, Moses sends scouts into the land, and renames one of them. In the King James: "And Moses called Oshea the son of Nun Jehoshua." Hoshea becomes Yehoshua, Joshua. A yud, added to the front. The lost letter found its place. Third, why tell it. It's a story about something small refusing to be wasted. The rabbis didn't let even one letter fall off the page and be forgotten. A lot of any day is yud-sized. A text answered. A dish washed. A name remembered. Small isn't the same as unimportant. The smallest letter begins the holy name.
screen: `IT BEGINS THE HOLY NAME.` · `SAID AS ADONAI, OR HASHEM.` · `SARAI'S YUD COMPLAINS.` · `HOSHEA BECOMES YEHOSHUA.` · then, large: `SMALL ISN'T UNIMPORTANT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: one small thing, done well. Settle, and breathe. Pick something tiny you'll do today anyway. Making the bed. Writing one line of a message. Pouring a glass of water. Folding one shirt. Now, in your mind, do it slowly and completely, the way a scribe forms a yud: not rushed, not careless, the whole of your attention on something nobody else may ever notice. Then let the picture go and just breathe. If you pray, you can offer that small act as part of your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Yud. The smallest letter, which begins God's holy name, and in the rabbis' story moved from Sarai's name to Joshua's. Today's word.
Your line: the smallest. Today, do the small thing you chose as well as you can, and don't tell anyone it took care. Day one thousand three hundred thirty-eight.

howItsDone: Jews traditionally do not pronounce God's holy name as written: in prayer and Torah reading it is read as Adonai, and in everyday speech some say Hashem, 'the Name'. Scribes writing a Torah scroll must form every letter, even the tiny yud, correctly.

original.note: Hebrew: the letter yud (י), the smallest letter, which begins God's holy name.

trapdoor: what you thought: yud is just a y, or a dot on the page.
what it means: the smallest letter, and the first letter of God's holy name.
what a scholar hears: the Jerusalem Talmud (Sanhedrin 2:6) tells that the yud taken from Sarai complained until it was added to Hoshea's name, making Yehoshua (Numbers 13:16).
recall: named for its first two letters

sources.quoted: And Moses called Oshea the son of Nun Jehoshua.

notes: Midrash of Sarai's yud: Jerusalem Talmud Sanhedrin 2:6 (also Bereishit Rabbah 47:1; Bavli Sanhedrin 107a has a related version). Paraphrased; 'for generations' is narrative. Confirm reference and summary.
'Smallest letter' and 'begins God's holy name' come from the index; the shape (hanging from the top line) is descriptive. Confirm.
Pronunciation customs (Adonai in prayer and Torah reading; Hashem in everyday speech; 'many say') stated as tradition. Confirm phrasing.
'The greatest name' at the end of the teach is a rhetorical superlative referring to God's name; now 'begins the holy name'.
Numbers 13:16 quoted from KJV (1769), which spells the names Oshea / Jehoshua. Confirm.
Joshua described as Moses' 'young assistant' (cf. Exodus 33:11, 'a young man'); confirm.

Editor: 'young assistant' (not in the cited Numbers 13) became 'one of the scouts' Moses sends, which Numbers 13:16 supports; 'for generations' softened to 'for a long time'; 'the smallest letter' in the teach framed as what tradition calls it; replaced the stock 'ordinary Tuesday' phrase.
